title: Keller monodromy is everything
W: Since 2026 there are polynomial maps of 3-space with constant nonzero Jacobian that are not invertible (counterexamples to the Jacobian conjecture), and every number n >= 3 of points in a generic fibre occurs. Show that for every n the fibre points can be permuted in every possible way by going around loops, i.e. the monodromy group can be the full symmetric group S_n.
M: Prove that for every $n\ge3$ there is a polynomial map $F:\mathbb C^3\to\mathbb C^3$ with $\det JF\in\mathbb C^{\times}$, of geometric degree $[\mathbb C(x):\mathbb C(F)]=n$, whose geometric monodromy group (the Galois group of the Galois closure of $\mathbb C(x_1,x_2,x_3)/\mathbb C(F_1,F_2,F_3)$, acting on the $n$ generic fibre points) is $S_n$.
why: After Alpöge's 2026 counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture in dimension 3, the natural invariants of a non-invertible Keller map are its geometric degree and the monodromy of its generic fibre; realising the full symmetric group in every degree would show these maps are as 'generic' as branched covers can be. It is a clean test of how flexible the new constructions are.
issues: Original M omitted the precise meaning of 'monodromy group' (now defined as the geometric Galois group). Literature (2026 preprints) already covers much of it: S_3 for Alpöge's map (arXiv 2607.20210, Thm 4.4); graded families with monodromy S_N for N=kd, k odd>=3, d>=3, and S_{2r-1} for r even (N = 3 mod 4), A_N in other cases, and S_12 for a quartic-seed member (arXiv 2608.02863); Gallagher's family realises every degree n>=3 but its monodromy is not computed; 'ordinary weighted lifts' have S_N monodromy by a Morse-degeneration argument (arXiv 2609.33491, Prop 7.1). Remaining cases (e.g. n=4,5,6,8,10) look routine: one transposition plus primitivity via a Morse degeneration of the fibre polynomial. Not elite; probably closes quickly.

title: Formal verification depth of RH
W: Is the Riemann hypothesis provable in very weak systems of arithmetic, such as elementary function arithmetic?
M: Decide whether the $\Pi^0_1$ form of RH (e.g. Lagarias' inequality $\sigma(n)\le H_n+e^{H_n}\log H_n$ for all $n$) is provable in $\mathrm{I}\Sigma_1$, or in $\mathrm{EFA}=\mathrm{I}\Delta_0+\exp$.
why: Friedman's 'grand conjecture' predicts that essentially all of ordinary number theory, RH included if true, is provable in EFA; RH is a concrete Pi^0_1 test case. But as a problem it is at least as hard as RH itself.
issues: Premise in W is false: RH has no Lean proof (2026 Lean work concerns zeta formalisation and a better critical-line proportion / 'quasi-RH', not RH). Fatal flaw: a false Pi^0_1 sentence is refutable already in Robinson's Q, so ANY resolution (provable, or unprovable i.e. consistent) implies RH is true. Hence the question strictly contains RH and, if RH is proved by ordinary means, the 'provable in EFA' direction is the expected routine bookkeeping covered by Friedman's grand conjecture. Not a reasonable list item.

title: Monochromatic square-sum triangles, many colours
W: Colour the positive integers with finitely many colours. Show there are always three different numbers of the same colour whose three pairwise sums are all perfect squares.
M: Prove that for every $r\ge1$ and every colouring $\chi:\mathbb N\to\{1,\dots,r\}$ there exist distinct $a,b,c\in\mathbb N$ with $\chi(a)=\chi(b)=\chi(c)$ and $a+b,\ a+c,\ b+c$ all perfect squares. (Equivalently: the triangle hypergraph of the graph on $\mathbb N$ with $a\sim b\iff a+b=\square$ has infinite chromatic number.)
why: Khalfalah and Szemeredi proved that every finite colouring has a monochromatic pair x != y with x+y a square; this asks for the next configuration, a monochromatic triangle in the 'square-sum graph'. Density arguments fail (residue classes such as n = 1 mod 3 contain no such triangle), so a proof must be genuinely Ramsey-theoretic, in the same family as the open Pythagorean-triple and {x,y,x+y,xy} problems.
issues: Statement clean; colouring renamed to chi to avoid a clash with the element c. Not found posed in the literature (checked Khalfalah-Szemeredi line, Pach's x+y=z^2 work, Di Nasso-Luperi Baglini style surveys). Local (p-adic) obstructions do not kill it: for each prime one residue/valuation class survives. Quick SAT check (CaDiCaL): a 2-colouring of {1..8000} avoiding such triangles exists, but none exists for {1..10000}, so the r=2 case holds with threshold in (8000,10000]; r>=3 is open computationally. Natural but somewhat specialised; B.

title: Computable connective constants
W: Count the self-avoiding walks of length n on the Cayley graph of a finitely generated group. Their n-th roots decrease to the connective constant, so it can always be approximated from above. For groups with a solvable word problem, can it always be computed to any precision, i.e. also approximated from below?
M: Let $G$ be a finitely generated group with solvable word problem, $S=S^{-1}$ a finite generating set, $c_n$ the number of $n$-step self-avoiding walks from $e$ in $\mathrm{Cay}(G,S)$, and $\mu(G,S)=\lim_n c_n^{1/n}=\inf_n c_n^{1/n}$ (a right-computable real). Is $\mu(G,S)$ always a computable real? If not, construct $(G,S)$ with solvable word problem and $\mu(G,S)$ non-computable. If so, is the map (word-problem algorithm, $S$) $\mapsto\mu(G,S)$ uniformly computable?
why: The connective constant is the basic growth rate of self-avoiding walks; for graphs with a (unimodular) graph height function, bridge counts are supermultiplicative and give matching lower bounds, so mu is computable for e.g. solvable groups with solvable word problem. Whether this can fail when no height function exists (Higman-type groups, torsion groups such as Grigorchuk's) ties the probabilistic theory of SAWs on groups to computability and symbolic dynamics, where entropies of effective subshifts are exactly the right-computable reals.
issues: Statement precise; inf=lim holds by submultiplicativity on transitive graphs. Known: mu is right computable for recursively presented groups (Aubrun-Bitar 2023, cited as Lemma 4.11 in arXiv 2402.13944); log mu is the entropy of the SAW 'skeleton' subshift; computable (Perron-number powers) for plain groups; lower bounds via bridges for Cayley graphs with graph height functions (Grimmett-Li), covering all f.g. solvable groups. The general question (left-computability without height functions) does not appear posed. A negative answer would need a group with solvable word problem whose SAW growth encodes a non-computable left limit, plausible via Dehn-monster or torsion constructions; neither direction looks easy. Specialised audience; B.

title: Three identical vortices on a square torus are chaotic
W: On a flat torus, three point vortices with total circulation zero form an integrable system (Stremler-Aref), but for vortices of equal strength even three are believed chaotic, from numerics only. Prove that three identical point vortices on the square torus are not integrable; the same question is open for four.
M: Let $G$ be the Green function of $\mathbb T=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z)$ ($\Delta G=\delta_0-1$) and $H=-\sum_{i<j}G(z_i-z_j)$ on $\{(z_1,\dots,z_N)\in\mathbb T^N: z_i\ne z_j\}$ with symplectic form $\sum_i dx_i\wedge dy_i$. The centre $Z=\sum_i z_i\in\mathbb T$ is conserved; the reduced space $M_N=\{Z=Z_0\}/(\tfrac1N\mathbb Z[i]/\mathbb Z[i])$ is symplectic of dimension $2N-2$. Prove that for $N=3$ the reduced flow on $M_3$ has no real-analytic first integral functionally independent of $H$ (and likewise for $N=4$ on $M_4$).
why: Point-vortex systems are the standard finite-dimensional models of 2D Euler; integrability is classified on the plane, sphere and for zero total circulation on the torus, but for nonzero circulation on the torus the translation momenta do not commute and only N=2 is integrable. Proving non-integrability for N=3 identical vortices would be the first rigorous chaos result for vortex lattices, where only numerics (Borisov-Mamaev-Kilin) exist.
issues: W's premise was false for identical vortices: Stremler-Aref integrability of three vortices in a periodic parallelogram requires zero total circulation; with nonzero total circulation only N=2 is integrable (survey arXiv 2003.00716, Thm 7) and N=3 is numerically nonintegrable (Borisov-Mamaev-Kilin, RCD 2019). Hence the original 'four identical' version skipped the first open case; restated with N=3 as main case. Clarified the reduction: Z in T is a genuine conserved quantity, translation by 1/N-lattice points acts on its level set, reduced dimension 2N-2 (P_x,P_y do not Poisson-commute, so translations remove only one degree of freedom). Also fixed Green-function normalisation (uniform background). Likely approach: Ziglin/Morales-Ramis along a collinear or symmetric invariant family, or Melnikov splitting; technical but feasible.

title: Translative Lebesgue covering
W: Find the convex shape of least area that contains a translated copy of every planar set of diameter 1, when only translations (no rotations or reflections) are allowed. Is the Jung disc of radius 1/sqrt(3), which is optimal for perimeter, also optimal for area?
M: Let $\mathcal D$ be the family of planar sets of diameter at most $1$. Determine $\alpha=\min\{\mathrm{area}(K): K\subset\mathbb R^2 \text{ convex},\ \forall X\in\mathcal D\ \exists t\in\mathbb R^2: X+t\subseteq K\}$ and all minimisers up to translation. In particular decide whether $\alpha<\pi/3$ (the area of the disc of radius $1/\sqrt3$).
why: Lebesgue's universal-cover problem (rigid motions allowed) is a century old and still unsolved; the translation-only version is the natural rigid analogue of Pal's solution of the convex Kakeya problem (equilateral triangle of height 1) and of Bezdek-Connelly's theorem that the disc of radius 1/sqrt3 is the unique minimum-perimeter translation cover of diameter-1 sets. Its answer measures how much rotation actually helps in Lebesgue's problem.
issues: Original title 'Hexagonal' was unjustified: a fixed regular hexagon of width 1 does not contain translates of all rotated Reuleaux triangles (Pal's hexagon argument uses rotation). Uniqueness claim replaced by 'determine all minimisers up to translation' (uniqueness unproven and unmotivated). Existence of a minimiser follows from Blaschke selection. Literature: perimeter version solved (Bezdek-Connelly; cited in arXiv 1209.2171); area version for diameter-1 sets not found solved; related translation/discrete-rotation covers for curves and segments in Jung-Yoon-Ahn-Tokuyama (Adv. Geom. 2023). Bounds: alpha >= area of min translation cover of unit segments and unit disc together; alpha <= pi/3. Quick numerics: translating 6 rotated copies of the width-1 Reuleaux triangle by optimized offsets gives hull area ~0.978 < centred 1.026, so the centred disc is likely not area-optimal, i.e. the answer is probably a non-trivial shape.

title: Firebreak with wind
W: A fire starts at a point and spreads faster downwind: its front moves at speed a + b cos(theta) in direction theta (0 <= b < a). Firefighters can build a barrier at total rate sigma (length per unit time), anywhere, and the fire cannot cross it. For which sigma can the fire be confined to a bounded region?
M: Let the reachable set of the free fire from $R_0=\{0\}$ be $tF$, where $F=\{r(\cos\theta,\sin\theta): 0\le r\le a+b\cos\theta\}$ (convexified if necessary), $0\le b<a$. A barrier is a rectifiable set $\Gamma=\bigcup_t\gamma(t)$ with $\mathcal H^1(\gamma(t)\cap\overline{R(t)})\le\sigma t$ (Bressan's admissibility), where $R(t)$ is the set reachable from $R_0$ by paths with velocity in $F$ avoiding $\Gamma$. Determine $\sigma^*(a,b)=\inf\{\sigma: \exists$ admissible $\Gamma$ with $\bigcup_t R(t)$ bounded$\}$, or at least its asymptotics as $b/a\to1$.
why: This is the anisotropic (wind-driven) version of Bressan's fire-confinement problem, whose isotropic threshold is still open (conjectured sigma* = 2, known only 1.626 <= sigma* <= 2). Wind is the realistic case for wildfires and makes the geometry of optimal barriers genuinely asymmetric.
issues: Original M was ill-posed: fire origin, wind direction relative to the town, where/when the barrier may be built, and what 'protects' means were unspecified. In its natural reading it is near-trivial: since an unconfined fire eventually covers the plane, the cheapest protection is a closed curve around the convex town, so the minimal length is essentially its perimeter whenever the time budget allows, and otherwise infeasible. Replaced by the anisotropic blocking-threshold question. That version is meaningful but derivative: it contains the open isotropic case (b=0) and anisotropic convex speed profiles are already in Bressan's framework (differential inclusions with convex velocity sets), so it is unlikely to be novel or elite.

title: Spikes at the primes
W: Put a bump of fixed height at every prime on the half-line lattice and study the electron (discrete Schrodinger operator). What kind of spectrum does it have inside the free band (-2,2)? If the primes behaved like a random sparse set (Cramer model), the states would be localized (pure point spectrum); is that true for the actual primes?
M: Let $(Hu)(n)=u(n+1)+u(n-1)+\lambda\mathbf 1_{\mathbb P}(n)u(n)$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$ with Dirichlet condition $u(0)=0$, $\lambda\ne0$. Determine the spectral type of $H$ on $(-2,2)$. In particular: is the spectral measure restricted to $(-2,2)$ pure point (with exponentially or sub-exponentially decaying eigenfunctions), or does it have a singular continuous part, e.g. near $E=0$?
why: It is the cleanest deterministic test of whether the primes are 'pseudo-random' for spectral theory: the random sparse model with site density 1/log n localizes, while deterministic sparse potentials typically produce singular continuous spectrum. The answer must use arithmetic input (distribution of primes in residue classes and gaps), linking Schrodinger operators to analytic number theory.
issues: No absolutely continuous spectrum is automatic: 1_P takes finitely many values and is not eventually periodic, so Remling's theorem (Annals 2011) gives Sigma_ac = empty; hence the content is pure point vs singular continuous. The conjectured pure-point answer is doubtful: numerics in the 2001 study 'De(Localization) in the Prime Schrodinger Operator' (cond-mat/0103313) report a persistent delocalized band near E=0 of width ~1/lambda. Simple check: at E=0 the recursion decouples by parity and, since all primes but 2 are odd, solutions grow only like partial sums of chi_4(p) (polynomially), not like the random model; analogous arithmetic resonances occur at E=2cos(pi a/q). So 'prove pure point' was replaced by 'determine the spectral type'. The question is posed (numerically) in the literature, so novelty is low; difficulty likely very high. Literature search for rigorous results was cut short by the search budget.

title: Heat with a cosine reaction
W: In u_t = u_xx + cos(x) u^2 the reaction term averages to zero over a period, but a second-order (homogenization) effect produces an effective +u^3 term, which in one dimension is exactly Fujita's borderline exponent where every positive solution of u_t = u_xx + u^3 blows up. Does every positive solution of the cosine equation blow up in finite time?
M: Prove or disprove: for every $u_0\in C_c(\mathbb R)$ with $u_0\ge0$, $u_0\not\equiv0$, the classical solution of $u_t=u_{xx}+\cos(x)\,u^2$, $u(\cdot,0)=u_0$, blows up in finite time. (More generally, for $a\in C^\infty(\mathbb T^d)$ with $\int a=0$, $a\not\equiv0$, show the Fujita exponent of $u_t=\Delta u+a(x)u^p$ is $p^*=1+1/d$: all positive solutions blow up for $1<p\le p^*$, small ones are global for $p>p^*$.)
why: Fujita's theorem is the prototype of 'all solutions blow up vs. small data global' thresholds; with a sign-changing, mean-zero weight the first-order effect cancels and the threshold is set by a homogenized second-order term $c\,v^{2p-1}$ with $c=\langle a,(-\Delta)^{-1}a\rangle>0$, predicting $p^*=1+1/d$. The posed equation is exactly the critical case $d=1,p=2$, where standard test-function/Kaplan arguments fail because the weight changes sign.
issues: Well-posed: positivity is preserved (linear comparison with coefficient cos(x)u), and large data blow up by comparison with the Dirichlet problem on (-pi/3,pi/3) where cos >= 1/2, so only small/spread data matter. Checked the homogenization: u ~ v + cos(x)v^2 gives effective v_t = v_xx + v^3 (coefficient 2<cos^2>=1), first-order oscillatory corrections average out, and next-order terms are integrable in time against the t^{-1} log-divergence of the critical case, so the conjectured answer is 'yes, all blow up'. Added the general-d, general-p formulation. Known results I recall (Pinsky 1997 for a(x) ~ |x|^m >= 0; Meier on bounded domains) do not cover periodic mean-zero weights; literature check was limited because the search budget ran out, so novelty is moderately uncertain.

title: Strauss exponent for an oscillating source
W: The 3D wave equation with source |u|^p has small-data global solutions exactly when p exceeds the Strauss exponent 1+sqrt2. If the source is multiplied by cos t, the usual blow-up proofs (which need a positive source) break, and time-oscillation may cancel the source. What is the new threshold?
M: For $u_{tt}-\Delta u=\cos(t)\,|u|^p$ on $\mathbb R^{1+3}$, $p>1$, with data $(u,u_t)(0)=\varepsilon(f,g)$, $f,g\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$, let $p_c=\inf\{p>1:$ for all $f,g$ the solution is global for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0\}$. Determine $p_c$, and show that for $1<p<p_c$ there are $f,g$ for which global existence fails for all small $\varepsilon$ (or the lifespan is finite). Is $p_c=2$ (parametric-resonance prediction) rather than $1+\sqrt2$?
why: Strauss' conjecture (now a theorem) is a central small-data threshold for nonlinear waves; all blow-up proofs use positivity of the source, so a sign-changing time-periodic factor tests which mechanism really sets the threshold. Heuristics suggest a different answer from Strauss, governed by resonance between the forcing frequency and the waves rather than by the size of the source.
issues: Original M presupposed a sharp dichotomy exponent (existence of p_c with blow-up below and global above), which need not hold; redefined p_c as an infimum and framed the blow-up side as failure of small-data global existence (growth could be infinite-time). Heuristics: near the light cone u ~ F(r-t)/r; integrating cos t |F|^p r^{1-p} along outgoing characteristics gives oscillatory cancellation, and the second-order averaged term (cos t * sin t) also averages to 0, so the Strauss/John iteration mechanism is suppressed. But |u|^{p-1} acts as a time-periodic potential cos(t) V with V ~ r^{1-p} on the shell, producing Mathieu-type resonance at frequency 1/2 with amplification exp(c int r^{1-p} dt), divergent iff p <= 2; this suggests p_c = 2, not 1+sqrt2. Not found in literature, but the search budget ran out before a dedicated search for time-dependent oscillating coefficients (literature on g(t)|u|^p usually takes g >= 0 or of power type), so novelty is uncertain.
